# AZ-104 Practice App: Complete Build, Deployment and Sync Guide

**Project date:** 6 October 2026  
**Platform used:** Windows, PowerShell, Python and a web browser  
**Deliverable:** a self-contained HTML practice app with 585 original questions, hosted on Azure Static Web Apps, with optional GitHub Gist progress sync

## 1. What this document contains

This is both a project history and a practical reconstruction guide. It records the requirements, design decisions, implementation, question-writing process, quality fixes, commands, tests, Azure deployment instructions and GitHub Gist configuration discussed in the chat.

**You can reconstruct the app using this Markdown file alone.** Appendix C contains a compressed archive encoded as text inside this document. It holds the complete source, all 585 questions, the two original built HTML files, the original browser test, its eight screenshots, and additional reconstruction helpers. Section 5 explains how to extract it. No access to the original chat, an AI agent, or a code repository is required.

There are three important boundaries:

1. **Exact artifact reconstruction is supported.** The archived original files are restored byte-for-byte and checked against SHA-256 hashes. Regenerating the same questions with an AI would not reliably produce identical wording, so the actual bank is included instead.
2. **This is not a verbatim transcript of every internal tool call.** Earlier messages were compacted. The surviving chat, checkpoints, source files and test output establish the sequence and major commands, but not every intermediate command, discarded draft or writer's individual research request. Unknown details are identified rather than invented.
3. **Cloud resources and personal progress are not included.** You must create your own Azure resource and GitHub token. The user reported successful Azure deployment; the chat did not supply the live URL, subscription ID, resource identifiers, deployment logs, token values, or confirmation that Gist sync succeeded. No credentials or personal progress are packaged.

The guide uses the following labels:

- **Recorded:** an action, result or decision evidenced by the conversation or original files.
- **Reconstruction:** a step added to make the project reproducible from this document.
- **Recommendation:** advice, not an official requirement or an action proven to have occurred.
- **Not verified:** an outcome that was not tested or confirmed in the chat.

## 2. What was built

The finished app is a browser-based AZ-104 study tool. All application code, styles, study content and questions are embedded inside a single HTML file. It does not need a server-side application or database to run practice sessions.

| Item | Final result |
|---|---|
| Original question bank | 585 questions |
| Domains / skill groups / objectives | 5 / 15 / 82 |
| Question-data files | 83 JSON files; one objective is split into a pilot and a continuation |
| Domain practice | 25 questions from one selected domain |
| Full practice exam | 50 questions with fixed per-domain quotas |
| Timer | None |
| Question types | Single-choice and multiple-answer |
| Completion tracking | A separate `Mark as Complete` checkbox |
| Local persistence | Browser `localStorage` |
| Optional cross-device sync | A secret GitHub Gist |
| Hosting chosen | Azure Static Web Apps, Free plan |
| Main HTML | `dist\az-104-practice.html` |
| Hosting entry point | `dist\index.html`, an identical copy |
| Original size per HTML file | 5,050,676 bytes, approximately 4.82 MiB |
| Bank version | `3b7a833e27` |
| Original build date | `2026-10-06` |

| Domain | Official weight used in the blueprint | Full-practice quota | Final bank size |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1: Manage Azure identities and governance | 20-25% | 12 | 165 |
| D2: Implement and manage storage | 15-20% | 10 | 136 |
| D3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources | 20-25% | 12 | 168 |
| D4: Implement and manage virtual networking | 15-20% | 9 | 64 |
| D5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources | 10-15% | 7 | 52 |
| **Total** | | **50** | **585** |

**Not an exact replica of the live Microsoft exam:** Microsoft does not publish a fixed AZ-104 question count. The recorded research said most Microsoft certification exams have 40-60 questions; 50 was an app-design assumption. The app's domain proportions sit within the recorded official weight ranges. It does not reproduce case studies, hot-area interactions, drag-and-drop items or practical exam labs. Its multiple-answer grading is all-or-nothing, not Microsoft's partial-credit system.

The app can run from a locally saved file without internet for ordinary study. Gist sync and external Microsoft Learn links require internet. A hosted page must first be downloaded; there is no service worker guaranteeing that a previously visited hosted page can be reopened offline. Keep a local HTML copy if offline availability matters.

## 3. Requirements and original decisions

### 3.1 Review first; do not build yet

The user initially supplied `gh-600-practice.html` and requested a review only. Building AZ-104 was explicitly deferred.

The review established a useful reference design:

- Approximately 858 KB, with 690 questions.
- A self-contained HTML document.
- Embedded JSON in a script element named `question-data`.
- Data fields including `blueprint`, `research`, `questions`, `sources` and `bankVersion`.
- A vanilla JavaScript app using URL hashes for navigation.
- Home, practice, results, review, question-library and study views.
- Browser-local persistence and export/import.
- Single-choice, multiple-answer and fill-the-gap formats in the reference.
- Clawpilot theme variables.

The AZ-104 app followed the self-contained architecture and study-oriented interaction model, not every feature of the reference. In particular, AZ-104 uses only single-choice and multiple-answer questions. The reference attachment is not necessary to rebuild the completed AZ-104 app and is not embedded here.

### 3.2 Who supplies the content?

The user asked whether they needed to provide domain names, a question bank or a study guide. The agreed approach was to obtain official exam objectives from Microsoft Learn, write original practice questions and create the study guide without requiring user-supplied educational content.

### 3.3 Original questions, not exam dumps

The user initially requested every possible question previously asked in AZ-104. This was adjusted: real exam items are confidential, and the project would not reproduce or reconstruct them. Instead, it would cover every objective in the official skills outline with original scenarios, explanations and source links.

This distinction is essential: **585 original questions is the delivered bank, not an exhaustive catalogue of real examination questions.**

### 3.4 Practice modes and feedback

Two modes were agreed:

1. Select a domain and receive 25 questions from that domain.
2. Receive a mixed 50-question practice exam using the domain quotas in Section 2.

No timer was requested or added. Domain practice defaults to feedback after checking each answer; full-exam practice defaults to feedback at the end. Options retain their original letters because the explanations refer to those letters.

### 3.5 Answer structure

Every question was required to include all ten sections, in this order:

| Section | Required purpose |
|---|---|
| Correct Answer | Start with the direct answer and identify the correct option(s) |
| Technical Explanation | Explain rules, evaluation order, scope, inheritance, precedence and exceptions where applicable |
| Why Every Other Option Is Wrong | Explain each wrong option separately, name the misconception, and say when it could be correct |
| In Plain English | Re-teach the concept to a reader without an IT background |
| Real-World Analogy | Map analogy parts to actual Azure components and explain where the analogy breaks down |
| Jargon Buster | Define terms, acronyms, products, roles, settings and commands |
| Watch Out / Good to Know | Highlight exam traps, exceptions, risks and limitations |
| Real-World Production Tip | Separate documented behaviour from practitioner recommendations |
| Memory Trick | Give a safe mnemonic and identify simplifications |
| Exam Tip | Explain clue words, elimination strategies, the distinction being tested and harder variations |

Assumptions and official sources follow the ten sections, so the UI displays twelve expandable sections in total.

Other rules included accuracy, internal consistency, gradual complexity, no filler, no assumed jargon knowledge, explicit assumptions, current official-source checks, and no invented Azure features or commands.

### 3.6 Hosting and progress sync

The user chose **Azure Static Web Apps** for hosting and **GitHub Gist** for sync. GitHub Pages was discussed as an alternative but was not used. Azure Functions plus Table Storage was discussed as a more involved backend alternative but was not built. Manual export/import was retained as a fallback.

A self-contained file cannot automatically share browser-local storage across devices. Gist provides an external place to store progress without creating an Azure application backend. The hosted page calls GitHub's API from the browser.

The Azure hosting location and GitHub progress storage are independent: **Gist sync does not require GitHub Pages.**

### 3.7 Hands-on labs were deferred

The user decided to practise questions first and build domain-specific labs later. No lab infrastructure or lab guide was created. A separate practice subscription, budget alert, one resource group per lab, and explicit cleanup were suggested for later work; these are recommendations, not deployed resources.

### 3.8 Credit-saving scope change

The initial targets totalled 703 questions:

- D1: 15 objectives at 11 questions each = 165.
- D2: 17 objectives at 8 each = 136.
- D3: 24 objectives at 7 each = 168.
- D4: 13 objectives at 10 each = 130.
- D5: 13 objectives at 8 each = 104.

The user became concerned about AI credit usage. The agreed reduction was to let already-running writers finish, then write the remaining 24 objectives at four questions each. Those were eleven remaining D4 objectives and all thirteen D5 objectives.

The two already-started networking objectives retained ten questions each. Final D4 therefore became `2 x 10 + 11 x 4 = 64`, and D5 became `13 x 4 = 52`. The final total was **585**, not the approximate 520 predicted in an interim update.

The blueprint's `target` values were originally planning metadata and remain the original targets. The UI calculates actual counts from the question bank rather than these targets. They are not evidence of missing runtime questions, and changing them is not required to reproduce the original.

## 4. Tools, accounts and terminology

### 4.1 Where each tool is installed

All development and upload commands run **on your Windows computer**, not inside the Azure portal or on your phone.

| Tool/account | Where it is used | Why it is needed |
|---|---|---|
| Windows PowerShell | Your computer | Enter commands to extract, build, test and upload |
| Python | Your computer | Extract the archive, validate questions and build HTML |
| Node.js | Your upload computer | Runs Microsoft's Static Web Apps command-line tool |
| npm | Installed with Node.js | Installs the upload tool |
| SWA CLI (`swa`) | Installed using npm | Uploads the `dist` folder to Azure |
| Python Playwright + Chromium | Your computer, only for browser testing | Runs the automated UI test |
| Azure account and subscription | Azure portal | Creates the hosting resource |
| GitHub account | GitHub website | Owns the Gist and sync token |
| Modern browser | Laptop, phone, tablet | Runs the finished app |

**Recorded versions:** Node.js `v22.17.1`, npm `10.9.2`. Documentation-time inspection also found Python `3.12.10`; that is a reconstruction reference, not proof of the Python version at every earlier action. The archive manifest records the installed Playwright version when available. The original npm install was unpinned; the exact SWA CLI version used for deployment was not recorded.

You do not need React, Vite, Tailwind, Azure CLI, Git, GitHub Actions, a GitHub repository, Azure Functions or a storage account for the chosen implementation/deployment path.

### 4.2 Basic terms

- **HTML:** the file format for a web page.
- **CSS:** rules controlling visual appearance.
- **JavaScript:** code executed by the browser.
- **JSON:** a structured text format used for questions and progress.
- **Self-contained:** application assets are inside one file, rather than fetched from several files.
- **Source:** editable files used to generate the finished HTML.
- **Build:** combining source and content into finished output.
- **`dist`:** the output folder uploaded to Azure.
- **Command-line tool / CLI:** a program controlled by typed commands.
- **`cd` / `Set-Location`:** changes the folder in which commands operate.
- **Resource group:** an Azure container for related resources; creating it alone is not a hosting fee.
- **Subscription:** the Azure account boundary for resources and billing.
- **Origin:** a browser security boundary made from protocol, hostname and port.
- **`localStorage`:** browser storage associated with an origin; not automatically shared with another device or browser.
- **Token:** a secret credential allowing a program to perform permitted actions.
- **Gist:** one or more files stored in a GitHub account.
- **Secret Gist:** unlisted, but readable by anyone who obtains its URL; not a private encrypted database.
- **SHA-256:** a checksum used here to detect any difference between file bytes.
- **Base64:** a way to store binary bytes as printable text.
- **ZIP:** a compressed archive containing multiple files.
- **URL hash:** the part after `#`; this app uses it to choose a screen without requesting another server page.

Save this complete file as **`AZ-104-COMPLETE-GUIDE.md`** in your Windows **Downloads** folder. If it downloaded somewhere else, move it there using File Explorer. Do not save only the introductory text or copy a truncated preview: the embedded archive at the bottom is required.

### 5.2 Choose a new workspace

We use `AZ104-Recreated` under your user folder. The extractor refuses to overwrite an existing folder so you cannot accidentally replace prior work.

The original chat used:

```text
C:\Users\v-ashrestha\.copilot\chats\2026-10-06\musical-system-a125f49d\az104
```

That original personal path is historical context, not a requirement. The new workspace works independently.

### 5.3 Create the extractor

The following PowerShell block creates a small local Python file. That Python file reads the archive inside this document, checks its hash, checks each file's hash and writes the verified contents into a new folder.

**Reconstruction helper:** this extractor was added for the documentation request. It was not part of the initial app implementation.

Paste this whole block into PowerShell:

```powershell
@'
import base64
import hashlib
import io
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import sys
import zipfile

if len(sys.argv) != 3:
    raise SystemExit("Usage: python restore-az104.py GUIDE.md NEW_DESTINATION")
document = Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig")
destination = Path(sys.argv[2]).resolve()
if destination.exists():
    raise SystemExit("Destination already exists. Choose a new empty location.")
begin = "<!-- AZ104_ARCHIVE_" + "BEGIN -->"
end = "<!-- AZ104_ARCHIVE_" + "END -->"
if document.count(begin) != 1 or document.count(end) != 1:
    raise SystemExit("Missing or repeated archive markers; use the complete Markdown file.")
block = document.split(begin, 1)[1].split(end, 1)[0]
match = re.search(r"```base64\s*\n([A-Za-z0-9+/=\r\n]+)\n```", block)
if not match:
    raise SystemExit("Archive block is missing or malformed.")
payload = base64.b64decode(re.sub(r"\s+", "", match.group(1)), validate=True)
expected_archive = "f4ecf408bf7eab18e19427d7bf5e7b7486327523d93282e10c571c92f37c7909"
if hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest() != expected_archive:
    raise SystemExit("Archive checksum mismatch: the document is incomplete or modified.")
verified = {}
with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(payload)) as archive:
    names = archive.namelist()
    if len(set(names)) != len(names):
        raise SystemExit("Archive has duplicate file names.")
    manifest_bytes = archive.read("MANIFEST.json")
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_bytes)
    if set(names) != set(manifest["files"]) | {"MANIFEST.json"}:
        raise SystemExit("Archive inventory differs from manifest.")
    for name in names:
        if "\\" in name:
            raise SystemExit("Unsafe archive path.")
        relative = Path(*name.split("/"))
        target = (destination / relative).resolve()
        if relative.is_absolute() or not target.is_relative_to(destination):
            raise SystemExit("Unsafe archive path.")
        content = archive.read(name)
        if name != "MANIFEST.json":
            entry = manifest["files"][name]
            if len(content) != entry["bytes"] or hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest() != entry["sha256"]:
                raise SystemExit("File checksum mismatch: " + name)
        verified[target] = content
for target, content in verified.items():
    target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target.write_bytes(content)
print(f"Restored {len(verified)} verified files to {destination}")
print("Project folder:", destination / "az104")
'@ | Set-Content -LiteralPath "$env:USERPROFILE\restore-az104.py" -Encoding UTF8
```

Then execute it:

```powershell
python "$env:USERPROFILE\restore-az104.py" "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\AZ-104-COMPLETE-GUIDE.md" "$env:USERPROFILE\AZ104-Recreated"
```

Expected result: a message reporting that the verified files were restored. If you receive a missing-file error, check the Markdown filename and download location. If the destination already exists, use a different new name, such as `AZ104-Recreated-2`, rather than deleting existing work.

## 6. Source structure and architecture

### 6.1 File responsibilities

| File | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `AUTHORING.md` | Full question-writing contract, schema and quality requirements |
| `blueprint.json` | Exam title, outline date, domains, weights, groups, objectives, targets and exam quotas |
| `research.json` | Exam facts, learning paths, study plan, exam technique, references and methodology |
| `questions\*.json` | Original prompts, options, answer keys, ten explanations, assumptions and sources |
| `validate.py` | Validates schema, minimum depth, wrong-option coverage, sources and repeated boilerplate |
| `src\template.html` | Page shell, navigation, theme scripts, data/script placeholders and dialogs |
| `src\style.css` | Responsive appearance and Clawpilot theme variables |
| `src\core.js` | Data maps, safe Markdown renderer, persistence, grading, sampling and Gist operations |
| `src\views.js` | Shared question/explanation rendering, overview and practice views |
| `src\views2.js` | Results, review, question library and progress views |
| `src\views3.js` | Study guide, sync screen, router, finishing sessions and confirmation dialog |
| `src\events.js` | Form, checkbox, navigation, import/export, keyboard and startup event handlers |
| `build.py` | Validates and combines the content and source into both finished HTML files |
| `gen.sql` | Historical generation-tracking helper, not a runtime database |
| `tests\e2e.py` | Original automated browser regression test, relocated into the portable archive |

### 6.2 Why vanilla JavaScript?

The goal was one portable HTML file, similar to the reference. A vanilla JavaScript app avoided a runtime framework dependency and a frontend package build pipeline. The HTML-artifact guidance's React pipeline was not used; its mandatory Clawpilot visual theme was retained.

The large initial attempt to write the entire app in one operation exceeded an output limit. Splitting JavaScript into five files kept creation manageable. The build concatenates them in this order:

```text
core.js -> views.js -> views2.js -> views3.js -> events.js
```

The files are ordinary scripts sharing one browser scope after concatenation, not independent ES modules.

### 6.3 Theme and layout

The template starts with theme detection using a `scoutTheme` URL parameter or the system light/dark preference. A second script applies a locally saved preference when no URL override is present. The Theme button stores the preference under `az104-theme`.

CSS uses the Clawpilot `--cp-*` variables for colours, including warm light backgrounds, dark charcoal surfaces and a rose accent. The exact stylesheet is included in the archive, so reproducing colour values by hand is unnecessary. Typography uses the Segoe UI/Aptos/Calibri family and Consolas for code.

Examples to force a theme:

```text
https://YOUR-SITE.azurestaticapps.net/?scoutTheme=dark
https://YOUR-SITE.azurestaticapps.net/?scoutTheme=light
```

### 6.4 Routes

| Hash | Screen |
|---|---|
| `#home` | Overview, domain selection, full-practice start and resume |
| `#practice` | Current practice session |
| `#results` | Completed-session score and breakdown |
| `#review/0` | Review question at zero-based position 0 |
| `#library` | Searchable question bank |
| `#progress` | Completion, accuracy, history, export/import/reset |
| `#study` | Study guide |
| `#study/facts` | Study guide, scrolled to exam facts |
| `#sync` | Gist token connection and sync status |

Unknown routes fall back to the overview. Because navigation uses hashes, server-side routing configuration is not needed.

### 6.5 Embedded data and build safety

The finished HTML stores JSON inside `<script id="bank" type="application/json">`. The top-level payload holds:

```text
blueprint, research, questions, bankVersion, builtOn
```

The build escapes closing-tag patterns in JSON so a question's text cannot prematurely close its script container. It also rejects literal closing script/style sequences in the source parts.

Question IDs are stable, such as `D1.2.2-01`. The objective prefix maps each question to its group and domain. The build sorts by numerical objective components, then question number.

The bank version is the first ten hex characters of SHA-256 over a canonical JSON representation of the questions. It is a bank-content version, not a hash of the full HTML and not a version of every UI file.

### 6.6 Rendering question Markdown

The app uses a small Markdown renderer rather than loading a third-party library. It supports paragraphs, bold, italic, inline code, single-level lists, small headings, pipe tables, fenced code blocks and HTTPS links.

It escapes HTML before rendering supported formatting. Raw HTML is prohibited in authored questions. Unsupported formats such as nested lists or images should not be used.

### 6.7 Sampling and grading

Question pools are grouped by objective. Sampling proceeds round-robin across those groups to encourage broad coverage. The optional preference for incomplete questions prioritizes questions not yet marked complete.

Domain practice draws 25 from the selected domain. Full practice samples each domain's quota, combines the selections and shuffles question order. **Question order is randomized; option order is not.**

For multiple-answer questions, the answer must contain exactly the correct set of option IDs with no duplicates. Extra or missing selections make the response incorrect.

In immediate-feedback mode, checking an answer records the attempt and locks its options. In end-feedback mode, answers remain editable until finishing. Finishing adds a history entry and counts unanswered items as wrong in the practice-session score. Unanswered questions do not create attempted-answer statistics.

### 6.8 Local state

Browser keys:

| Key | Contents |
|---|---|
| `az104-state-v1` | Completion flags, attempts, history, current session and optional reset timestamp |
| `az104-gist-v1` | Token, Gist ID, GitHub login and last successful sync time |
| `az104-theme` | Light/dark preference |

The primary state structure is:

```text
{
  v: 1,
  completed: { questionId: { done, at } },
  stats: { questionId: { n, correct, last, at } },
  history: [finished-session summaries],
  session: current-session-or-null,
  resetAt: optional-ISO-timestamp
}
```

History is limited to 500 entries. Session state holds IDs, answers, checked items, flags, index, feedback mode and timestamps. Import/load sanitizes state against the known question map and supported structure.

Completion is deliberate and separate from correctness: answering correctly does not automatically tick `Mark as Complete`.

### 6.9 Gist synchronization protocol

The progress filename is **`az104-progress.json`**.

Connection and sync use:

1. `GET /user` to identify/validate the token owner.
2. `GET /gists?per_page=100&page=N` to find a Gist containing that filename.
3. If none is found, `POST /gists` with `public: false` to create a secret Gist.
4. `GET /gists/{id}` to read remote progress.
5. Merge local and remote state.
6. `PATCH /gists/{id}` if the merged progress differs from the remote document.

The app searches up to ten pages of 100 Gists. If multiple Gists contain the filename, auto-discovery uses the first match. An explicit Gist ID avoids ambiguity.

The app uses GitHub JSON API headers and the recorded API version `2022-11-28`. That is the original implementation, not a claim that it is GitHub's newest API version.

If GitHub marks the file as truncated, the app fetches its `raw_url`. The token is sent to `api.github.com`; the raw-content fetch does not attach the authorization header.

Automatic sync occurs:

- On opening the app when connected.
- About 2.5 seconds after a persisted change, using a debounce.
- When the page becomes visible again.
- When the browser reports it is online again.
- When the user clicks **Sync now**.

There is no continuously running background service or real-time push subscription. A closed browser cannot sync.

### 6.10 Merge rules and their limitations

| State item | Merge rule |
|---|---|
| Completion | Latest timestamp per question wins, including unticking |
| Attempt statistics | Latest timestamp per question wins; counters are not added across simultaneous edits |
| Finished-session history | Union by session ID, sorted newest first, limited to 500 |
| Current session | Later `updatedAt` wins |
| Reset | Latest `resetAt` removes older completion, stats, history and sessions |

This is a lightweight personal sync approach, not a transactional collaborative database. Simultaneous updates from two devices can race between read and write. Two independently active sessions can replace one another. Device clocks influence timestamp ordering. Sequential use and syncing before switching devices reduce conflicts.

## 7. Research and question-bank authoring

### 7.1 Official outline and research

**Recorded:** the outline used was **skills measured as of 17 April 2026**, researched in October 2026. The source was Microsoft's official AZ-104 study guide.

Research covered the certification page, skills outline, learning paths, course page, exam duration/experience, scoring, practice assessment, sandbox and renewal.

The recorded study guide includes:

- 100 minutes to answer; 120-minute seat time quoted for associate exams without labs.
- Typical Microsoft exam question range of 40-60, not a fixed AZ-104 count.
- Passing scaled score of 700 or more; not equivalent to a 70% practice score.
- No penalty for guessing.
- Possible partial credit and unscored items in the real exam.
- Microsoft Learn availability with restrictions and without stopping the exam clock.
- Break restrictions and inability to return to previously seen questions after a break.
- Ten listed exam languages.
- Retake and annual renewal information.

These are historical research results, not permanent guarantees. The app links to official sources so the reader can check current policies.

The prerequisites learning-path identifier was corrected during research to:

```text
az-104-administrator-prerequisites
```

All seven learning/course links in `research.json` were reported to return successfully at the time.

### 7.2 Blueprint construction

`blueprint.json` was created with five domains, fifteen skill groups and eighty-two objectives. IDs such as `D3.4.8` identify an objective within a domain/group.

The per-domain exam quotas were configured as 12, 10, 12, 9 and 7. Initial authoring targets were 11, 8, 7, 10 and 8 questions per objective for D1 through D5 respectively.

Appendix B supplies the full outline and actual counts, rather than requiring the reader to infer them from names or external pages.

### 7.3 Authoring specification and pilot

`AUTHORING.md` established the rules before bulk writing. It specifies:

- Original scenarios only.
- Verify Azure facts against `learn.microsoft.com`.
- Prefer generally available behaviour and label previews.
- Use current names such as Microsoft Entra ID.
- State cloud/region/licensing/default-setting assumptions.
- Cite official sources.
- Aim for approximately 20% multiple-answer questions.
- Aim for a foundation/applied/advanced difficulty mix of approximately 20%/55%/25%.
- Avoid implausible distractors and `all/none of the above`.
- Keep option lengths comparable and spread correct-answer letters.
- Use the supported Markdown subset.
- Write all ten required answer sections.
- Separate official behaviour from recommendations.

The first pilot was four questions for `D1.2.2`. It passed validation. A continuation file, `D1.2.2-part2.json`, added IDs `-05` through `-11`, so that objective ultimately has eleven questions.

### 7.4 Exact question schema

This describes the format; the complete actual question content is embedded in the archive.

```json
{
  "id": "D1.2.2-01",
  "objective": "D1.2.2",
  "type": "single",
  "difficulty": "applied",
  "prompt": "Original scenario and question in supported Markdown",
  "options": [
    {"id": "A", "text": "First option"},
    {"id": "B", "text": "Second option"},
    {"id": "C", "text": "Third option"},
    {"id": "D", "text": "Fourth option"}
  ],
  "correct": ["B"],
  "assumptions": "Explicit assumptions",
  "sections": {
    "correctAnswer": "Direct answer",
    "technical": "Technical explanation",
    "wrongOptions": {
      "A": "Misconception: ... Could be correct when: ...",
      "C": "Misconception: ... Could be correct when: ...",
      "D": "Misconception: ... Could be correct when: ..."
    },
    "plainEnglish": "Re-explanation",
    "analogy": "Analogy and where it breaks down",
    "jargon": [{"term": "A term", "definition": "Its meaning"}],
    "watchOut": "Traps and limits",
    "productionTip": {
      "official": "Documented behaviour",
      "recommendation": "Practitioner recommendation"
    },
    "memoryTrick": "Mnemonic with qualifications",
    "examTip": "Clues and distinctions"
  },
  "sources": [
    {"title": "Official source title", "url": "https://learn.microsoft.com/..."}
  ],
  "verified": "2026-10"
}
```

This is a schema illustration, **not a valid finished practice question**: it intentionally does not meet the content-length thresholds. Real files hold arrays of fully written questions. For multiple-answer questions the prompt must explicitly say `Select TWO` or `Select THREE` as appropriate.

### 7.5 Parallel writing process

After the pilot, writers were launched by objective:

1. Wave 1: eight writers for D1.1.1-D1.1.5, D1.2.1, the D1.2.2 continuation and D1.2.3.
2. Wave 2: twelve writers for D1.3.1-D1.3.7 and D2.1.1-D2.1.5.
3. Further batches completed D2.2.x, D2.3.x and D3.
4. Work continued with roughly twelve single-objective writers at a time.
5. After the credit-saving decision, twelve paired writers handled the last twenty-four objectives at four questions per objective. Already-running writers finished their original targets.

Each writer was instructed to read the authoring spec and pilot, stay inside its assigned objective, plan distinct sub-concepts, verify official sources, save JSON, run validation and fix errors. Its completion report identified the file, question count and any unverifiable facts omitted.

A portable prompt for future additions is:

```text
Read AUTHORING.md completely and follow it.
Read questions\D1.2.2.json as a worked example.
Write N ORIGINAL questions for objective <ID>: <official objective name>.
Stay inside this objective and test a different sub-concept per question.
Use stable new IDs that do not conflict with the existing bank.
Verify facts against official learn.microsoft.com pages.
Do not use real exam items, dumps, copied practice tests or filler.
Write every answer section specifically for its own scenario.
Save a UTF-8 JSON array in questions\<new-file>.json.
Run python validate.py questions\<new-file>.json and fix all errors.
Report the filename, count and unverifiable facts you omitted.
```

**Recommendation:** no new AI generation is needed to recreate this project; use the packaged bank to avoid extra credits and non-deterministic output.

### 7.6 Generation tracking

A session SQL table tracked `objective`, `name`, `target`, `agent` and `status`. Status was changed to running when assigned and done after validation.

Examples of recorded tracking queries:

```sql
UPDATE gen SET status='running', target=4 WHERE status='pending';
UPDATE gen SET status='done' WHERE objective='D3.3.3';
SELECT status,count(*) FROM gen GROUP BY status;
```

A mistaken update referenced an `id` column that did not exist and returned `no such column: id`; the corrected query used `objective`.

The twenty-four reduced objectives initially remained marked pending despite their writers running; their records were corrected. The durable `gen.sql` is a historical helper, not a dependency for build, hosting or sync. You do not need a SQL server.

### 7.7 Quality problem and corrective changes

An early 88-question bank passed the initial schema checks, but inspection found reused generic sentences and analogy tables in D1.1.1, D1.1.3, D1.1.4, D1.2.3 and some D1.2.1 material.

This met a minimum length while violating the user's no-filler requirement. The response was to strengthen both the spec and validator:

- A no-templated-text rule was added to `AUTHORING.md`.
- A `boilerplate()` check rejects a sentence or table row of at least 50 characters reused in three or more questions in the same file.
- A depth check rejects questions below 800 counted words across the prompt and serialized answer sections.
- Affected writers were asked to rewrite question-specific content, not pad text.
- Subsequent writers were explicitly warned about repetition.

The authoring target is 900-1600 words; 800 is the automated minimum, not the ideal.

The repetition detector is **per file**, not a semantic duplicate detector across the whole bank. Passing it does not prove all content is unique, pedagogically excellent or factually correct.

### 7.8 Validator rules

| Rule | Automated requirement |
|---|---|
| Required fields | ID, objective, type, difficulty, prompt, options, correct, assumptions, sections, sources, verified |
| Objective | Must exist in blueprint |
| ID | Must start with objective plus `-` |
| Options | 2-6, sequential letters, nonempty text |
| Single-answer key | Exactly one correct option |
| Multiple-answer key | At least two valid distinct correct options, matching selection wording |
| Wrong-option explanations | Exactly one for every wrong option and none for correct options |
| Wrong-option wording | Must mention a misconception and when the option could be correct |
| Analogy | Must identify where it breaks down |
| Jargon | At least four entries with term and definition |
| Production tip | Both official and recommendation text, at least 80 characters each |
| Sources | At least one titled `https://learn.microsoft.com/` URL |
| Total minimum depth | 800 counted words |
| Repeated boilerplate | No qualifying long unit reused in 3+ questions in a file |
| IDs across provided files | No duplicates |
| Raw HTML / all-none choices | Rejected by pattern checks |

Section minimum lengths are measured in **characters**:

| Section | Minimum |
|---|---|
| Correct Answer | 40 |
| Technical Explanation | 400 |
| In Plain English | 250 |
| Real-World Analogy | 200 |
| Watch Out | 120 |
| Memory Trick | 40 |
| Exam Tip | 200 |

The validator checks structure and patterns; it does not fetch sources itself, verify every command, prove that all jargon is defined, or certify factual accuracy. Those remained authoring/review responsibilities.

### 7.9 Facts omitted because writers could not verify them

The recorded omissions were:

| Objective | Claim not used without verification |
|---|---|
| D1.2.1 | Numeric role-assignment limits |
| D2.1.1 | A claim that `/30` is unsupported; recorded docs referred instead to `/31` and `/32` |
| D2.1.4 | Retirement date of Key Vault managed storage account keys |
| D2.2.5 | AzCopy `--dry-run` and changing access tier through Storage Explorer |
| D2.3.6 | A 48-hour lifecycle delay; recorded docs described 24 hours |
| D3.2.6 | Exact SLA percentages, with questions referring to the relevant SLA source |
| D3.3.2 | `gitRepo` volume deprecation |
| D3.4.4 | Uploaded PFX certificate minimum key-size claim of 2048 bits |

These are historical verification gaps, not assertions that every omitted claim is false. Do not add them back without current official evidence.

Another scope correction told the D3.4.3 writer not to make deployment-slot swapping its main concept because D3.4.8 specifically covers slots. This reduced overlap between objectives.

```text
585 questions, 0 errors

Correct-option occurrence counts:
```

The original duplicate-prompt check normalized non-word characters and compared the first 120 characters of prompts. It did **not** prove the absence of semantic near-duplicates. Earlier shorthand statements such as "no duplicates" should be read in that narrower sense.

The answer-letter spread was inspected but not perfectly balanced or changed. Multiple-answer questions contribute more than one letter occurrence, and many questions have only A-D options, so the numbers do not total 585.

## 9. Validate and build the app

### 9.1 Enter the project folder

```powershell
Set-Location "$env:USERPROFILE\AZ104-Recreated\az104"
```

This makes commands such as `python .\build.py` refer to the restored project.

### 9.2 Validate one question file

```powershell
python .\validate.py .\questions\D1.2.2.json
```

Expected last line:

```text
4 questions, 0 errors
```

Why: this checks a small file when editing one objective rather than repeatedly testing the entire bank.

### 9.3 Validate the full bank

```powershell
$questionFiles = (Get-ChildItem .\questions\*.json).FullName
python .\validate.py @questionFiles
```

Expected final line:

```text
585 questions, 0 errors
```

If you changed content and get errors, fix the named question/file before building.

### 9.4 Run the additional portable bank audit

**Reconstruction helper:** this was added for the document to make the earlier count/duplicate checks repeatable.

```powershell
python .\tools\audit_bank.py
```

It checks total/domain/objective counts, duplicate IDs, normalized full prompts and the original 120-character normalized-prefix rule, prints the letter spread, and recomputes the bank version. It does not replace technical fact-checking.

### 9.5 Normal build

```powershell
python .\build.py
```

What it does:

1. Finds all question JSON files.
2. Runs `validate.py`.
3. Rejects duplicate IDs or objectives absent from the blueprint.
4. Sorts questions.
5. Computes the bank version.
6. Creates a payload with blueprint, research, questions and build metadata.
7. Inlines CSS, JavaScript and data into the HTML template.
8. Writes `dist\az-104-practice.html` and identical `dist\index.html`.

**Date caveat:** a normal rebuild uses today's date. If you run it on another day, its footer and `builtOn` differ from the original, even if the question bank is unchanged.

`--force` exists and was available during in-progress writing. It bypasses validation failures and can skip unreadable JSON. Do **not** use it for a final or production rebuild; it can publish incomplete content.

### 9.6 Byte-exact historical rebuild

**Reconstruction helper:** to reproduce the original build date without changing your Windows clock:

```powershell
python .\tools\build_recorded.py
```

This invokes the unchanged original `build.py` with its date source fixed to `2026-10-06`, still runs validation, and compares both outputs with the original hashes. It restores the original result exactly when the archived source is unchanged.

Expected message:

```text
Both HTML files match the recorded SHA-256.
```

A mismatch is an explicit failure, not a successful reconstruction. If you intentionally edited the app or bank, use the normal build instead.

### 9.7 Inspect the outputs

```powershell
Get-ChildItem .\dist | Select-Object Name, Length
Get-FileHash .\dist\az-104-practice.html -Algorithm SHA256
Get-FileHash .\dist\index.html -Algorithm SHA256
```

The original byte count is 5,050,676 for each file. Appendix A records the exact original SHA-256. Both hashes should be equal.

In PowerShell window A:

```powershell
python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory .\dist
```

Why: the browser test expects `http://127.0.0.1:8765/az-104-practice.html`. Binding to loopback keeps this test server accessible only from your computer.

Leave this window running. Open the URL in a browser. In window B, you can verify response:

```powershell
(Invoke-WebRequest "http://127.0.0.1:8765/az-104-practice.html" -UseBasicParsing).StatusCode
```

Expected: `200`.

**Recorded historical command:** `python -m http.server 8765` was run in `dist`; the loopback bind above is a safer reconstruction recommendation.

The app build uses only Python's standard library. The optional browser test needs Playwright and its Chromium browser.

If already installed, there is no need to reinstall. The archive records the documentation-time Playwright version; for an equivalent installation you may pin that version from `MANIFEST.json`.

In PowerShell window B:

```powershell
python .\tests\e2e.py .\tests\new-shots
```

The test uses an isolated browser context, not your regular browser's progress. It captures eight screenshots. Expected final output:

```text
ERRORS: none
```

Recorded coverage included:

- Initial completion count.
- Domain practice has 25 items.
- Explanation shows ten sections plus assumptions and sources.
- Checked answers lock.
- Flagging.

**Test limitations:** the original script only asserts at least twelve full-exam questions, not exactly fifty or every domain quota. It also prints failed checks and `ERRORS` but does not set a nonzero process exit code. Read its output rather than assuming exit code zero means all assertions passed. ### 10.6 JavaScript syntax check

The original app was syntax-checked with `node --check`. Since its source parts form one script, concatenate them in build order for a portable repeat:

```powershell
$parts = 'core.js','views.js','views2.js','views3.js','events.js'
$joined = ($parts | ForEach-Object { Get-Content (Join-Path .\src $_) -Raw }) -join "`n"
```

No output and a successful exit indicate syntactically valid JavaScript. This is not a browser behaviour test.

Return to PowerShell window A and press **Ctrl+C**. This stops only the server you launched.

## 11. Deploy to Azure Static Web Apps

### 11.1 Cost boundary

**The chosen hosting resource can be free:** use **Azure Static Web Apps Free**, the supplied Azure hostname and HTTPS, no extra backend, and no paid add-ons.

The earlier statement "there is nothing that can be charged" was too broad for an entire Azure subscription. Free Static Web Apps does not make unrelated resources, future labs, bought domain names, DNS services, paid support, paid plans or AI authoring credits free.

Official quotas checked for this guide:

| Free-plan limit | Recorded value |
|---|---|
| Included monthly bandwidth | 100 GB |
| Paid bandwidth overage | Unavailable on Free |
| Single-environment storage | 250 MB |
| Total storage across environments | 500 MB |
| Static Web Apps per subscription | 10 |
| Preview environments per app | 3 |

The two HTML files total 10,101,352 bytes. A rough uncompressed comparison puts 100 GB at about 20,000 full 5 MB downloads, but compression, caching and other traffic change actual usage. This is an estimate, not a promised number of visits.

Do not assume exceeding a quota silently upgrades the app or adds paid bandwidth: Free has no paid overage option. Check current service restrictions if quotas become relevant.

### 11.2 Create the hosting resource

Perform these steps in your browser:

1. Open <https://portal.azure.com> and sign in.
2. Search for **Static Web Apps**.
3. Open the service and click **Create**.
4. Select the Azure subscription you intend to use.
5. For **Resource group**, create one named `rg-az104-practice`, or use your chosen equivalent.
6. For **Name**, enter `az104-practice`, or your chosen name.
7. Set **Plan type** to **Free**. Do not select Standard or another paid plan.
8. Under **Deployment details**, set **Source** to **Other**.
9. If a region is requested, choose an offered region suitable for you.
10. Click **Review + create**.
11. Review the subscription, plan and resource details carefully.
12. Click **Create**.
13. Wait for deployment to finish, then click **Go to resource**.

Portal labels can change. The important settings are the Free plan and the manual/Other deployment source. No GitHub repository connection, GitHub Actions workflow, application build configuration or API configuration was part of this deployment.

The names above were examples suggested in the conversation, not confirmed names of the user's actual deployed resource.

### 11.3 Get the Azure deployment token

1. Open your Static Web App resource.
2. On **Overview**, choose **Manage deployment token**.
3. Copy the token.
4. Keep it private.

This token lets the upload tool deploy to that particular Static Web App without a normal interactive Azure sign-in. Someone with it can replace your site.

**This is not the GitHub token.** Azure's token is for uploading the site; GitHub's token is for saving progress. Never put either token into the HTML source, question bank, documentation or a repository.

### 11.4 Install the upload tool on your Windows computer

Open PowerShell on the computer that holds `dist`.

```powershell
npm.cmd install -g @azure/static-web-apps-cli
swa.cmd --version
```

Explanation:

- `npm` is installed with Node.js.
- `install` downloads/installs a package.
- `-g` makes its commands available from other folders.
- `@azure/static-web-apps-cli` is Microsoft's upload-tool package.
- `swa` is the command that package provides.

The original chat used `npm install -g ...` and `swa ...`; `.cmd` invokes the Windows command launcher explicitly and avoids PowerShell `.ps1` execution-policy issues. This is a reconstruction convenience, not a different deployment method.

The global tool installation is normally a one-time step. The app itself does not use Node.js in Azure.

### 11.5 Upload the finished files

First enter the project folder:

```powershell
Set-Location "$env:USERPROFILE\AZ104-Recreated\az104"
Get-ChildItem .\dist
```

The original command pattern was:

```text
swa deploy .\dist --deployment-token <your-Azure-token> --env production
```

Do not type angle-bracket placeholders literally. Pasting a token directly into a command can retain it in shell history. The following recommended alternative keeps the token out of the command text by setting the officially supported process environment variable:

```powershell
$secret = Read-Host "Paste the AZURE deployment token" -AsSecureString
$pointer = [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($secret)
try {
    $env:SWA_CLI_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN = [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($pointer)
    swa.cmd deploy .\dist --env production
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "Deployment failed. Read the tool output before retrying." }
}
finally {
    [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($pointer)
    Remove-Item Env:\SWA_CLI_DEPLOYMENT_TOKEN -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    Remove-Variable secret,pointer -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
```

Why the flags and paths matter:

- `.\dist` means the built-output folder below the current folder.
- The deployment token authenticates the upload.
- `--env production` targets the main live environment; the CLI's default is preview.
- `index.html` allows Azure to serve the app at the site root.

The token necessarily exists in process memory/environment during deployment. The secure prompt reduces accidental history disclosure; it is not protection against malicious software or an administrator on your machine.

### 11.6 Open and verify the live site

1. Return to the resource's **Overview**.
2. Open the **URL** displayed there.
3. Confirm the overview loads and the footer shows 585 questions and bank version `3b7a833e27`.
4. Start one domain practice and confirm there are 25 navigation dots.
5. Start a full practice and confirm there are 50.
6. Open the same URL on your phone to inspect the responsive layout.

The URL will resemble `https://SOME-GENERATED-HOST.azurestaticapps.net`. The resource name is not necessarily the site's exact hostname; use the URL Azure supplies.

**Recorded outcome:** the user explicitly reported that Azure Static Web App deployment succeeded. The agent did not inspect the deployed resource or independently verify the user's live URL.

### 11.7 Updates

For later changes:

1. Edit the source or question JSON, keeping stable IDs where the same questions remain.
2. Validate.
3. Build normally.
4. Upload `dist` again using the same method and an active deployment token.
5. Reload the live page; use Ctrl+F5 on Windows if needed.

No source files, screenshots, Markdown guide, local token files or progress exports need to be uploaded. Deploy only `dist`.

## 12. Configure GitHub Gist sync

### 12.1 What this adds

Hosting makes the app accessible from several devices, but each browser still has independent local progress. Gist sync copies and merges that progress through your own GitHub account.

You need a GitHub account and a fine-grained personal access token granting **Gists: Read and write**. You do not need a GitHub repository or GitHub Pages.

### 12.2 Create the token

1. On your laptop, open <https://github.com>.
2. Sign in to the account that should own your progress.
3. Open <https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new>.
4. Confirm the heading is **New fine-grained personal access token**.
5. Enter **Token name:** `az104-gist-sync`.
6. Leave **Description** blank, or add `Sync my AZ-104 practice progress`.
7. For **Resource owner**, select your personal account.
8. For **Expiration**, choose 90 days if available, or an appropriate custom date.
9. Under **Repository access**, leave **Public repositories** selected. This does not grant private-repository write access; the app does not require repository permissions.
10. Scroll to **Permissions**.
11. Under **Account permissions**, find **Gists**.
12. If necessary, click **Add permissions**, select **Gists**, then configure it.
13. Set **Gists** to **Read and write**.
14. Leave unrelated optional permissions unselected / No access. If GitHub displays mandatory built-in read-only access, do not try to remove platform-required defaults.
15. Click **Generate token** and confirm if asked.
16. Copy the token immediately; GitHub only shows its full value once.
17. Save it in a password manager if you need to connect other devices later.

**Screenshot context:** the user's screenshot showed resource owner `lepcheone`, a 30-day expiry selected initially, Public repositories selected, and no token generated yet. The instructions told that user to retain their personal resource owner and choose 90 days or a custom expiry. Use your own account when recreating.

A fine-grained token typically begins `github_pat_`. Do not share the full token in chat, screenshots, email or this document.

**Permission scope warning:** Gists read/write is not limited to just this app's one Gist. It permits operations on the owner's Gists within that permission. Use trusted personal devices only.

### 12.3 Connect the laptop first

1. Open your deployed Azure Static Web App URL.
2. Click **Sync** in the app's navigation.
3. Paste the GitHub token into **Fine-grained personal access token**.
4. Leave **Gist ID** blank on the first connection.
5. Click **Connect and sync**.
6. Wait for successful status such as **Last synced ... as YOUR-ACCOUNT**.
7. Note the displayed **Gist ID**.
8. Optionally click **open on GitHub** to see `az104-progress.json`.

The app finds or creates the Gist automatically. Do not upload the practice HTML to a Gist: the Gist stores progress, not the 5 MB application.

### 12.4 Connect a phone or another device

1. Open the same HTTPS website on that device.
2. Open **Sync**.
3. Securely retrieve the same token from your password manager.
4. Paste it into the token field.
5. Leave Gist ID blank to auto-discover, or paste the exact ID shown on the laptop to avoid ambiguity.
6. Click **Connect and sync**.
7. Confirm the same account and Gist are shown.

A different token per device is possible if each token belongs to the same GitHub account and grants the same Gists permission. The original simplest instruction was to use the same token on each device.

### 12.5 Verify end-to-end sync

**Not verified in the original chat:** no successful real Gist connection or two-device sync result was reported. Perform this acceptance check:

1. On the laptop, mark one identifiable question complete.
2. Click **Sync now** and wait for a successful timestamp.
3. On the phone, return to the app and click **Sync now**.
4. Find the same question and confirm its completion checkbox is ticked.
5. Untick it on the phone and sync.
6. Return to the laptop, sync and confirm the untick arrived.
7. Check that both devices show the same Gist ID.

Repeat with a finished practice session if you want to confirm history sync. Prefer one device at a time for active practice sessions.

### 12.6 Expiry and disconnect

When a token expires or is revoked, local study still works, but sync fails. Create a replacement token with the same minimum permissions, then:

1. Export local progress as a precaution.
2. Open Sync and choose **Disconnect this device** if currently connected.
3. Reconnect using the replacement token and the recorded Gist ID.
4. Repeat on each device using that token.

Disconnect removes the browser's stored token/configuration, **not** the Gist or local progress. Revoking the token on GitHub prevents further use; it also does not delete the progress Gist.

### 12.7 Secret does not mean private

GitHub documents secret Gists as unlisted, not truly private. Anyone with the URL can read the file. It contains question IDs, timestamps, attempt counts, scores and possibly the unfinished practice answers/session.

The token is stored in browser local storage and is not part of the HTML or progress export. The Gist is not a place to put credentials or sensitive personal material. GitHub may retain Gist revision history, so resetting current progress should not be treated as secure erasure of old revisions.

## 13. Use the app

### 13.1 Domain practice

1. Open Overview.
2. Choose a domain.
3. Choose feedback mode if offered.
4. Keep the preference for incomplete questions if you want less repetition.
5. Start the practice.
6. Select an answer or the requested number of answers.
7. In study/immediate mode, click **Check answer**.
8. Read the explanations and source links.
9. Tick **Mark as Complete** when you deliberately consider that question studied.
10. Use Next, Previous, navigator dots or arrow keys to move.
11. Flag questions you want to revisit.
12. Finish and review the results.

Starting a new practice warns before replacing an unfinished session. Completion ticks and attempt statistics remain.

### 13.2 Full practice exam

Start full practice from Overview. Its default end-feedback mode withholds explanations until finishing. There is no countdown timer. You can flag and change answers before finishing.

The score is an ordinary practice percentage, not Microsoft's scaled score. The readiness recommendation of consistent 80% on fresh questions is advice, not an official pass threshold or a guarantee.

### 13.3 Question bank

Use **Question bank** to search and filter by domain, objective, completion/attempt state and other available filters. Search can match an ID prefix; `D1.1.3` yields eleven questions in the original bank.

The library initially renders forty entries and supports **Show more**. It fills an entry's body only when opened, avoiding rendering hundreds of long explanations at once. You can try an answer, reveal an explanation, retry and mark complete.

### 13.4 Progress and study guide

**Progress** shows completion totals, domain/objective breakdowns, accuracy and practice history. It provides export, import and reset.

**Study guide** shows exam facts, the outline with actual question counts, official learning paths, a recommended study plan, exam technique, references and limitations.

`Mark as Complete` is a self-assessed study milestone, not proof of proficiency. Attempt accuracy and full-practice results offer different signals.

## 14. Maintenance, backups and recovery

### 14.1 Export progress

1. Open **Progress**.
2. Click **Export**.
3. Save the downloaded JSON safely.

The filename resembles `az104-progress-YYYY-MM-DD.json`. It includes state, export time and bank version, but not the GitHub token. Back up before reset, browser cleanup, domain changes or significant app upgrades.

### 14.2 Import progress

1. Open the app on the destination browser.
2. Open **Progress**.
3. Click **Import**.
4. Select the exported JSON.
5. Confirm the completion/history totals.

Import merges by the same timestamp-oriented rules, rather than blindly replacing everything. An exported document older than a later reset may be filtered out by reset timestamps. Keep a backup, but do not promise that importing automatically reverses every reset.

### 14.3 Reset

Reset clears completion, stats, history and current practice after confirmation. When connected, the reset timestamp propagates to synced devices and prevents older state from being merged back.

It is not just a reset of the current laptop. Export first. Reset does not revoke a token or securely erase historical Gist revisions.

### 14.4 Preserve source and stable IDs

Keep the Markdown guide or extracted workspace in a safe backup location. Azure hosts the deployed output, not your complete editable project.

When revising an existing question, preserve its ID if it remains conceptually the same. Renaming/removing IDs can orphan completion entries or invalidate a saved session. The app keeps the same local-storage keys across bank builds; it does not have a full data-migration framework.

### 14.5 Moving the website

Moving from one hostname to another creates a new browser origin. Local storage and token setup do not automatically follow. Reconnect to the same Gist on the new site or export/import progress first.

Use the same canonical site URL across devices. `index.html` and `az-104-practice.html` served from the same origin share local storage, but a local `file:` copy and the hosted HTTPS site do not.

## 15. Troubleshooting

The table separates problems that actually occurred from additional recovery guidance.

| Symptom | Status | Cause/check | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single giant app write exceeded output limit | Recorded | Too much source in one generation operation | Split template/CSS/JS and concatenate at build |
| Generic explanations repeated across questions | Recorded | Minimum-length checks did not detect filler | Add boilerplate/depth gates, strengthen spec, rewrite affected questions |
| SQL `no such column: id` | Recorded | Tracking table used `objective`, not `id` | Correct the update predicate |
| Paired objectives still marked pending | Recorded | Assignment tracking was not updated | Mark the twenty-four assigned objectives running |
| D3.4.3 overlaps deployment-slot objective | Recorded | Wrong main sub-concept | Reserve slots for D3.4.8; use a different D3.4.3 concept |
| `npx playwright` not responding | Recorded | Exact underlying cause not established | Use available Python Playwright |
| Azure upload successful | User-reported | User completed instructions | No deployment fault reported |
| Gist connection successful | Not verified | User received setup steps only | Run the two-device acceptance check in Section 12 |
| `python` not found | Additional guidance | Missing install/PATH or Store alias | Install Python; reopen shell; try `py -3` |
| `npm`/`swa` not recognized | Additional guidance | Missing Node/tool or PATH refresh | Check Node/npm; install CLI; reopen shell |
| `npm.ps1`/`swa.ps1` cannot run | Additional guidance | PowerShell execution policy blocks script launcher | Use `npm.cmd` / `swa.cmd`; avoid unnecessary global policy changes |
| Extractor archive hash mismatch | Additional guidance | Truncated/modified Markdown | Obtain complete file; do not bypass checksum |
| Extract destination exists | Additional guidance | Overwrite protection | Choose a new folder |
| Build says validation failed | Additional guidance | Malformed/underdeveloped question content | Fix specific errors; do not deploy with `--force` |
| Playwright executable missing | Additional guidance | Browser bundle not installed | Run `python -m playwright install chromium` |
| Port 8765 already used | Additional guidance | Another process listening | Identify owner; stop only your server or use a port with corresponding test-URL changes |
| Azure invalid deployment token | Additional guidance | Wrong, expired/reset or copied incorrectly | Copy correct app's token; reset if compromised; retry |
| Upload went to preview | Additional guidance | Missing production option | Deploy again with `--env production` |
| Default Azure landing page remains | Additional guidance | Wrong output folder/site/environment or failed upload | Verify `dist\index.html`, production success and correct Overview URL |
| Browser still shows older app | Additional guidance | Cached HTML | Hard reload, verify footer version and deployment result |
| GitHub 401 | Additional guidance | Invalid/expired/revoked token | Create active token, reconnect |
| GitHub 403 | Additional guidance | Permissions, policy or rate limit | Read returned message; confirm Gists read/write; wait if rate-limited |
| GitHub 404 | Additional guidance | Wrong/deleted/inaccessible Gist or permissions | Confirm ID/account and access before allowing creation of a new Gist |
| Sync error while offline | Expected behaviour | No internet | Continue locally; reconnect and Sync now |
| Wrong Gist discovered | Additional guidance | Multiple Gists with `az104-progress.json` | Export local progress; reconnect with intended exact Gist ID |
| Progress seems absent on phone | Additional guidance | Different URL/browser/account/Gist; not yet synced | Check origin and Gist ID; Sync now on both |
| Progress gone after browser cleanup | Additional guidance | Local storage removed | Reconnect Gist or import backup |
| State alternates between two active devices | Additional guidance | Latest-session/timestamp merge conflicts | Use one active session at a time; sync between devices |
| Storage warning in app | Expected error path | Browser storage unavailable or full | Export; use trusted normal browser; enable storage or Gist |

For a browser API/network problem, open Developer Tools with **F12**, select **Network**, reproduce Sync now, and inspect the failed request's status and response. **Do not share Authorization headers or token values.**

No broad catch-all troubleshooting command should delete the workspace, clear all browser storage, or terminate all Python/Node processes. Recover the smallest relevant component.

## 16. Security, costs and known limitations

### 16.1 Token separation

| Credential | Purpose | Where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| Azure deployment token | Publish/replace Static Web App files | Upload computer during deployment |
| GitHub fine-grained token | Read/write progress Gists | Trusted browser on each connected device |

Neither is included in this guide or embedded archive. A token pasted into the browser is not automatically inserted into the publicly hosted HTML file.

However, local storage is readable by JavaScript executing on the site's origin. A compromised deployed page, malicious browser extension or compromised device can expose it. Keeping the deployment token private is therefore important not only for site integrity but also for connected users' browser-stored GitHub tokens.

### 16.2 Free hosting is a scoped statement

For this static page on the Free plan, with the Azure-provided hostname and no added paid services, hosting is intended to incur no Static Web Apps charge under the documented limits. It is not a promise that Azure pricing will never change or that your whole account can never be billed.

Manual CLI deployment avoids the GitHub Actions minutes/storage considerations associated with a repository-driven workflow. No paid custom domain was required. Node.js, the CLI and Python do not create Azure resources merely by being installed.

### 16.3 Quality and verification limits

- All 585 questions passed automated rules; those rules are not a complete factual audit.
- Writers reported verifying sources, but the chat does not contain an independently replayed verification of every assertion.
- Exact-ID and prompt-key duplication checks passed; semantic duplication was not exhaustively proven.
- Option-letter balance was inspected but not perfected.
- The original UI regression passed; real Gist connectivity and conflict behaviour were not tested against the user's account.
- The user's deployment was reported successful; no independent live-site inspection was recorded.
- The content reflects its recorded April/October 2026 outline/research snapshot; current official documentation takes precedence.
- The app does not implement the practical hands-on lab project deferred by the user.

### 16.4 Lightweight sync limitations

The implementation is intentionally simple and has no server-side access control for the public study page, no database transaction/locking, no continuously running worker and no proof against simultaneous-client overwrites.

If a remote Gist file is absent or cannot be parsed, the current implementation can treat remote state as unavailable and write local state. Before editing the Gist manually or recovering suspicious data, download/export a backup. This guide documents the existing behaviour; it does not silently change the app.

For personal study it can be convenient. For sensitive records, multiple collaborating users, strict audit requirements or robust concurrency, a purpose-built authenticated backend would be a different future project.

|---|---|---|
| Pilot/writers | `python az104\validate.py <question-files>` | Validate each completed objective before accepting it |
| Tracking | SQL updates keyed by `objective` | Track pending/running/done generation |

| Boilerplate fix | Edit spec/validator; ask affected writers to rewrite | Remove generic repeated explanations |
| Reduced generation | Four questions per remaining objective, paired writers | Respond to user's credit concerns |
| UI target check | Search source for `.target` | Confirm actual-count display does not rely on planning targets |
| Scratch cleanup | Remove temporary `pairs.json` | Remove generation-only pairing list |
| Final validation | Validate all 83 question JSON files | 585 questions, zero errors |
| Final audit | Python ID/prompt-prefix/letter/domain checks | No duplicate keys; domain counts recorded |
| Final build | `python build.py` from `az104` | Two 5,050,676-byte HTML files |
| Final UI check | Run original `e2e.py` against final output | `ERRORS: none` |
| Cleanup | Stop managed server and its identified port listener | Leave no test server running |
| Tool checks | `node --version`; `npm --version` | Node 22.17.1/npm 10.9.2 already installed |
| Upload instruction | `npm install -g @azure/static-web-apps-cli` | Install upload tool |
| Upload instruction | `swa deploy .\dist --deployment-token <token> --env production` | Publish main environment |
| User result | "azure static web app deployed" | Deployment success user-reported |
| Gist instructions | Fine-grained Gists read/write token, Connect and sync | Configuration provided; final success unreported |

### 17.4 Verification of this guide's reconstruction path

On 6 October 2026, the complete Markdown was generated and its embedded extractor was run into a new temporary folder. The checks below used that extracted copy, not the original working app:

1. All 111 archived files were restored and their manifest hashes checked.
2. The bank audit confirmed 585 questions, all 82 objectives represented, the five expected domain counts, no duplicate IDs or checked prompt keys, and bank version `3b7a833e27`.
3. The exact-date build ran validation and produced both original HTML files byte-for-byte. Their SHA-256 was `3fb6ccd93b353da37417434308c62e76e9dc2135ae8c25b22c91416a7a23ef8d`.
4. A loopback-only temporary server served the extracted app.
5. The added quota test passed all five 25-question domain checks and the exact 50-question mixed-exam distribution.
6. The original browser regression reported all checks passing and `ERRORS: none`.
7. The temporary server was stopped.

This verifies the local reconstruction/build/test workflow. It does not constitute a new Azure deployment or a real GitHub-token test.
